explainers.detection: Fires are detected from space by NASA FIRMS. Polar-orbiting satellites — VIIRS on NOAA-20/21 & Suomi-NPP, and MODIS on Terra/Aqua — scan Algeria several times a day, flag thermal hotspots and measure each fire's radiative power (heat output in MW). Data arrives near-real-time, about 3 h after the satellite passes.
explainers.confirmed: We then show only Confirmed fires: detections flagged high-confidence with a fire radiative power of 15 MW or more. This filters out low-confidence noise and small agricultural burns, leaving what is almost certainly a real, active wildfire.
explainers.fwi: The Fire Weather Index (FWI) rates how easily a wildfire could start and spread today — from the weather alone: heat, dryness, wind, and how long since it last rained. Higher means more dangerous conditions. It's the standard used by fire services and the EU (EFFIS). Note: it shows the risk, not that a fire is already burning.

methodology.title: About this data
methodology.b1: Detections are not area burned. We count satellite fire pixels and their radiative power (FRP), not hectares. A detection is a ~375 m (VIIRS) or ~1 km (MODIS) thermal signal, not a mapped burn scar.
methodology.b2: Coverage differs by sensor. VIIRS (375 m) data begins ~2012; MODIS (1 km) ~2000. Later years have more satellites and finer resolution, which inflates counts versus earlier years.
methodology.b3: Clouds, smoke and overpass timing cause undercounting. Satellites only see at pass times; a quiet day may mean poor viewing, not fewer fires.
methodology.b4: Recent data is near-real-time and may be revised; older data uses the science-quality archive.
methodology.b5: "Confirmed" means a high-confidence detection with FRP ≥ 15 MW, clipped to Algeria's borders. Persistent industrial gas-flares are largely excluded by this filter.
methodology.b6: One fire spans many pixels and passes — that is why we cluster detections into incidents. Counts are estimates, not an official tally.
